shortDescription: A bilingual northern Ontario regional city where lakes, strong seasons, public buses, English and French institutions, mining/service economies and durable civic programs shape ordinary life.
longDescription: The World is rooted in Greater Sudbury, Ontario, where a caregiver, step-caregiver and child share a small duplex while a close grandparent lives elsewhere in the city. English and French public life, GOVA transit, public schools, libraries, recreation programs and regional health/education services provide ordinary movement beyond the household. Mining and mining supply are visible parts of the city's economy without defining every family or future path, and Anishinaabe treaty-territory context is part of the public regional setting without assigning the subject an Indigenous identity. Across 2004–2026, phones and digital services change substantially while winter maintenance, lakes, strong seasonal light, buses and bilingual institutions remain persistent.

visualProfile.overallCharacter: An ordinary mid-sized northern Ontario city: modest residential streets, durable public institutions, strong seasons, bilingual civic cues and nearby lake/Canadian Shield geography without wilderness replacing city life.
visualProfile.geographyAndClimate: Northern Ontario lake region with snow and ice in winter, freeze/thaw shoulder seasons, warm green summers and large seasonal daylight differences; rock, lakes and forested edges are part of the city's physical setting.
visualProfile.builtEnvironment: Small duplexes and low-rise housing, publicly funded school campuses, GOVA bus stops/shelters, public-library spaces, recreation halls, health/service buildings, modest commercial areas and visible mining/service infrastructure in the wider city.
visualProfile.streetsAndPublicRealm: Residential sidewalks, plowed and salted winter streets, bus shelters, school grounds, library approaches, recreation facilities and ordinary commercial corridors; seasonal maintenance should be visually credible.
visualProfile.interiors: Practical duplex rooms, school labs/arts/workshop spaces, bilingual library reading/computer areas, recreation-hall rooms, community-program spaces and ordinary indoor gathering places during colder months.
visualProfile.materialsAndTextures: Wood siding or painted masonry, concrete, asphalt, snow/slush/salt grit seasonally, winter fabrics, laminate/wood public interiors, sports flooring, workshop materials, books and household utility objects.
visualProfile.lightAndAtmosphere: Low winter sun and blue-gray cold-weather light, snow-reflected brightness, warm indoor illumination, wet spring/fall conditions and long bright summer evenings; avoid permanent winter gloom.
visualProfile.vegetationAndLandscape: Deciduous and coniferous urban trees, ordinary yards and parks, exposed Canadian Shield rock and lakes visible in the regional environment; the city should still read primarily as inhabited urban life.
visualProfile.mobilityAndVehicles: Walking and GOVA buses are ordinary local mobility, with seasonally visible winter delays/maintenance; practical cars and service vehicles exist, while occasional intercity travel should remain secondary.
visualProfile.signageAndLanguage: English and French may both appear on municipal, library, school and service information. Depending on the specific institution, signage may be English, French or bilingual; do not force every sign to be duplicated for visual effect.
visualProfile.clothingAndEverydayObjects: Seasonally appropriate contemporary Canadian urban clothing; winter coats/boots/gloves when needed, school bags, transit passes/cards, phones, books, hobby/sports equipment, workshop tools and household heating/maintenance items.
visualProfile.technologyAndInfrastructure: School and public computers, household electronics, phones, transit information and internet access should evolve from 2004 to 2026; winter road maintenance, heating systems, buses, libraries and recreation facilities remain durable infrastructure.
visualProfile.publicInstitutions: Ontario public schooling including English/French board options, GOVA transit, Greater Sudbury Public Library, municipal recreation, community health services and local postsecondary programs should remain ordinary parts of the World.

temporalLayers.2004_2010: Flip/feature phones, desktop-heavy internet access, more paper schedules and older municipal/household electronics; buses, schools, libraries and winter infrastructure remain recognizable.
temporalLayers.2011_2018: Smartphones and Wi-Fi become ordinary, digital school/library access expands and transit information becomes more online while the same residential and seasonal structure persists.
temporalLayers.2019_2026: Contemporary smartphones, digital public-service interfaces and newer transit/commercial cues may appear; public institutions, bilingual services, strong seasons and modest housing remain visually continuous.
temporalLayers.continuities: English/French public life, winter snow and maintenance, GOVA buses, lakes/rock, schools, libraries, recreation programs and regional mining/service context remain durable anchors.
